rows.n: Chess Collection — Cleveland Public Library MAIN Library
rows.w:
This is the right building. The 1925 Main Library on Superior Avenue — not a branch, not the Louis Stokes Wing next door. Go in the Main Building, take the marble staircase to the third floor, and pass through the John Griswold White Exhibition Corridor (look for owls in the wrought-iron cases) into Special Collections.

Inside is the John G. White Chess and Checkers Collection: the largest chess collection in the world. Over 35,000 items going back to the 12th century — one-of-a-kind sets from every continent, rare manuscripts, Bobby Fischer score sheets, Lasker medals, the most comprehensive tournament records anywhere, and two death masks of Gisela Kahn Gresser, nine-time US women's champion. White was a Cleveland attorney who collected from 1870 until his death in 1928, buying up entire European and American chess libraries; the library has kept collecting since. It has been on this floor since the doors opened.

Five-story glass-roofed atrium built in 1890 as America's first indoor shopping centre, modelled on Milan's Galleria and financed in part by Rockefeller. Top three floors are now a Hyatt. A Superman film was shot here.
ph: Photo: Martin Linsey, HABS photographer · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: The 42nd floor of a 52-story tower that was briefly the world's second-tallest. Views across the bridges, the Cuyahoga and Lake Erie. Small and dated in a way that's part of the appeal.
ph: Terminal Tower from the Warehouse District
Photo: edseloh · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: Civil War memorial with a free museum inside — bronze reliefs, marble busts, knowledgeable volunteers. Beneath it runs a labyrinth of tunnels that opens to the public one day a year.
ph: Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument, Public Square, Cleveland
Photo: Cards84664 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen's giant rubber stamp, tipped on its side, reading FREE. Roughly 28 × 26 × 49 feet. Commissioned for a corporate plaza, rejected, then exiled here — arguably the better ending.
Pei's glass pyramid on the lakefront, five floors of exhibits. Even if you're not a devotee the history of how the music got made — and the DJs who took the risks — carries it.
ph: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame building, Cleveland (2016)
Photo: MusikAnimal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.w: The largest outdoor chandelier in North America, hung 44 feet above Euclid Avenue: 4,200 crystals, each placed by hand at roughly twenty minutes apiece. It anchors Playhouse Square, the largest performing arts centre in the United States outside Lincoln Center — five restored 1920s theatres saved from demolition by a volunteer campaign.

A 618-foot Great Lakes freighter tied up beside the Science Center, open stem to stern — engine room, pilot house, crew quarters and the panelled guest staterooms. The deck gives one of the better skyline views in the city.

rows.n: Hope Memorial Bridge & the Guardians of Traffic
rows.w: Eight art deco sandstone giants, each 43 feet tall, holding vehicles from a hay wagon to a 1930s truck — Henry Hering's Guardians of Traffic, carved into the bridge pylons in 1932. The baseball team took its name from them. Pedestrian walkways run both sides.

Formally "The Angel of Death Victorious." A life-size bronze on the Haserot family plot, holding an extinguished torch upside down. Decades of oxidation have left black streaks running from her eyes down her neck, so she appears to weep. Herman Matzen sculpted her; canning magnate Francis Haserot commissioned her after his wife died in 1919.

Vietnamese-owned and family-run in Asiatown, and by consensus the best phở in the city. The bone broth simmers 24 hours from a recipe passed down through the family; the owner is known to throw out an entire vat that doesn't meet standard. Fourteen versions of phở, plus bánh mì, bún thịt nướng, summer rolls and proper Vietnamese coffee.

Directly across from Presti's, and the rivalry is the point — go to both and pick a side. Corbo's does not pre-fill its cannoli shells, and is the place for cassata cake and sfogliatelle. Closed Monday.

Made on site in a restored 1920s cinema, with a glass wall so you watch the production floor while you eat. Lavender honey and the Cleveland brownie sundae are the ones people name. Two minutes from West Side Market.
Old Brooklyn institution since 1974, honey-sweetened, and the flavour Clevelanders grew up on. Orange blossom is the signature.
A Cleveland chocolate house since 1935, with a table-service ice cream parlour attached — pretzels come free with your sundae, for dipping in their hot fudge. Same road as Dang Good.

Organic, largely vegetarian and entirely made in house — coffee, pizza, salads, and live jazz some evenings. Composts everything. The best room on this side of town to sit in for two hours with nobody minding.
A full 1920s-style soda fountain rebuilt from scratch — marble counter, hand-pumped syrups, enormous sundaes, and a candy counter. The root beer float is the order.

rows.n: Li Wah — Cantonese dim sum carts
rows.w: Cantonese. Freshwater calls it the best dim sum in Cleveland and it is still the only place running proper steel carts at weekend lunch — har gow, siu mai, chicken feet, roast duck, rice rolls, circling the room. Hundreds of people pack it on Saturday and Sunday.

Cantonese / Hong Kong-style. Freshwater rates it the best Chinese restaurant in Asiatown and says some would extend that to all of Northeast Ohio. Roast duck and char siu hanging in the window, chive pot stickers, shrimp wonton noodle soup, three-flavour dumpling soup, salt-baked shrimp, soy sauce chicken, beef chow fun. Full-colour photos of nearly every dish cover three of the four walls.
Cantonese. The other dim sum house, and Cleveland Magazine's pick for late night — open past midnight, until 2am Friday and Saturday. Har gow and shrimp rice rolls get named repeatedly.

A counter and a few tables at the back of a grocery, inside a mall. Cleveland Scene sends people here for bún bò Huế — the spicy Huế beef noodle soup — and for shrimp wonton noodle soup loaded with pork dumplings and egg noodles. There's a bun bakery attached.
Sichuan. Cleveland Magazine calls it a favourite standby of Cleveland chefs. Cumin lamb skewers, scallion pancakes, and a spice level that is not adjusted for the room — mind the traditional dishes.
Taiwanese bakery and bubble tea, and where the Infatuation tells you to get a coconut cream bun after phở. Buns sweet and savoury, egg tarts, and the best boba in the city by most local accounts.

Cantonese seafood, despite the Thai name — thirty years in, live tanks, Hong Kong-style dishes, whole steamed fish, pork belly with preserved vegetable. Diners who know Cantonese cooking single out the fried clams for being fried properly.
A century-old Italian bakery and the anchor of Little Italy. Cannoli, sfogliatelle, lady locks, Linzer cookies, plus savoury Stromboli and artichoke pizza. Take a number or you will get cut in line.

Eastern European, run by three sisters across several generations of the same family. Wiener schnitzel, cevapi, stuffed cabbage, city chicken, dumplings and gravy, and homemade strudel. Cheap, slow, and exactly what people mourn now that Sokolowski's is gone.

Bourdain's favourite stop in Cleveland — chicken paprikash, stuffed cabbage, head cheese and boiled pig's head, served cafeteria-style. “This might be the greatest establishment ever,” he said. A James Beard America's Classic. It closed after 100 years in the same family. Listed so you know it is gone rather than wondering.

Bourdain ate here. He opened the 2007 No Reservations Cleveland episode with a three-way — spaghetti, cinnamon-spiced chili, shredded cheddar — explicitly to needle his Cleveland-native guide Michael Ruhlman, since Skyline is a Cincinnati thing. Clevelanders were furious. That is exactly why it's here.

rows.w: A grocery store inside the old Cleveland Trust Company bank rotunda — stained-glass dome, marble, murals. Go up to the balcony seating and eat lunch under it.

rows.n: Azure Rooftop Lounge at The 9 — CLOSED
rows.w: Twelve floors up, open air, skyline in every direction. Nothing hot on the menu — come for the view and a cold drink.
A community garden for motorcycle repair — shared tools, shared knowledge — that also has a bar and live music. Members bring in salvage bikes and rebuild them with help.
Seasonal, and non-negotiable if you're here in December. It isn't Christmas in Cleveland without it.

rows.n: The RainForest, Cleveland Metroparks Zoo — CLOSED
rows.w: A two-storey simulated Amazon under glass, with an open aviary you walk through, a pool where it rains on a schedule, and a fog that rolls off the water. Included with zoo admission; parking is free.

A Cleveland icon from April 1985 that covered 3.1 million miles over 37 years. It shut down permanently in May 2022. Listed here for completeness — Lake View Cemetery still runs its own trolley tours.

Vietnamese, family-run, and in the same room since 1984 — the oldest Vietnamese restaurant in Cleveland. The signature is the #21 cinnamon rare beef phở; regulars also come for the vermicelli with grilled pork, the crêpes (bánh xèo) and the homemade chilli oil.

Colombian-Venezuelan, and the arepa place Cleveland actually argues about — 3,300 reviews at 4.6. Arepas, cachapas, empanadas, birria arepa, and mojitos that people order first. Named repeatedly in Infatuation and Yelp's Venezuelan rankings.
